title: Cash, Cards, and ATMs in Korea: A Beginner's Guide to Paying for Things
html:
Korea is one of the most cashless-friendly countries in the world, but it isn't fully cashless — and the mix of cards, apps, and cash that actually works can be confusing the first time you visit. This guide walks through exchanging currency, using your foreign credit or debit card, and pulling out Korean won from an ATM, so you're not caught off guard at the register.

Should you exchange cash before you land?

Short answer: not much, if any. Exchange counters at your home airport, and even the ones inside Incheon Airport, almost always give a worse rate than what you'll get once you're actually in Korea. It's fine to bring a small amount of your home currency or US dollars for peace of mind — enough for a taxi or a snack right after landing — but there's no need to load up on won in advance.

Airport and home-country exchange counters tend to bake in a wide margin — you'll almost always do better waiting until you're in Korea. Photo: epSos.de, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. Source.

The two better options once you land: withdraw won directly from a Global ATM with your regular debit card (see below), or use a travel-friendly card like Wise or a similar multi-currency card, which converts at close to the real mid-market exchange rate instead of a marked-up "tourist" rate.

Exchanging cash once you're in Korea

If you do want physical cash, private money-changer shops beat both airport counters and banks on rate. The best-known cluster is in Myeongdong, a shopping district in central Seoul, where dozens of small currency exchange shops sit side by side and openly display their rates in the window — it's normal to compare a couple of shops before choosing one. For small amounts, many don't ask for your passport, but it's good practice to carry it anyway.

Myeongdong, in central Seoul, is the easiest place to find competitively priced currency exchange shops within walking distance of each other. Photo: ProjectManhattan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

Banks also exchange foreign currency, but expect to show your passport, possibly wait in a queue, and sometimes deal with more limited hours than a money-changer shop that's open into the evening. Unless you're exchanging a large amount, a Myeongdong-style shop or a Global ATM is usually simpler.

Card culture: what actually works in Korea

Visa and Mastercard are accepted almost everywhere a tourist is likely to shop or eat — department stores, cafes, convenience stores, chain restaurants, and most mid-size shops. Tap-to-pay (contactless) is common in Seoul, though you may still be asked to insert a chip card at some older terminals. UnionPay is also widely supported. A few things to know:

  • Small, family-run restaurants, traditional markets, and street food stalls are the places most likely to be cash-only, or to have a terminal that only reads Korean-issued cards. This gets more common the further you get from Seoul and Busan's main tourist areas.
  • Some shops prefer cash for purchases under roughly ₩10,000 to avoid card processing fees, even if they technically accept cards.
  • Check with your home bank before you fly — many cards charge a foreign transaction fee (often 1–3%) on every purchase made in Korea, which adds up over a trip.

Tap-to-pay is increasingly common in Seoul, but don't be surprised if a smaller shop asks you to insert your chip instead. Photo: Lmccart5, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Source.

What locals actually do: most Koreans pay with a domestic debit or credit card tapped through Kakao Pay, Naver Pay, or Samsung Pay, all linked to a Korean bank account. As a short-term tourist you generally can't sign up for these, since they require a Korean phone number and a local ID number. The closest tourist-friendly equivalent is WOWPASS, a prepaid card you top up with foreign cash or card at orange kiosks found in airports and major subway stations — it works on Korea's domestic payment network, so it's accepted at places that sometimes reject foreign Visa or Mastercard, and it doubles as a T-money transit card.

Getting cash from ATMs (look for the "Global ATM" label)

If your card is on the Visa, Mastercard, Plus, Cirrus, or UnionPay network, you can withdraw won directly from machines marked "Global ATM" — look for the sticker or an English-language screen option. Two main types:

  • Convenience store ATMs at CU, GS25, 7-Eleven, and Emart24 — open 24 hours and everywhere, though fees run a bit higher, typically around ₩3,000–₩3,600 per withdrawal on top of whatever your home bank charges.
  • Bank ATMs, especially KEB Hana Bank and Woori Bank, which tend to charge some of the lowest fees for foreign cards (roughly ₩3,500–₩4,000), and are found at most bank branches nationwide.

Major Korean banks like KB Kookmin, Shinhan, Woori, and KEB Hana all run Global ATM networks that accept foreign cards. Photo: Parkso123, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Source.

Withdrawal limits are usually around ₩300,000 per transaction at a convenience store machine, and higher at a bank branch. If a machine rejects your card, it doesn't always mean something is wrong with your account — try a different bank's ATM before assuming the worst.

Practical tips

  • Carry roughly ₩50,000–₩100,000 in cash as a backup, more if you're planning to visit traditional markets, small towns, or street food alleys outside Seoul.
  • A multi-currency travel card (like Wise) plus one Global ATM withdrawal early in your trip covers most travelers well — card for daily spending, cash for the places that need it.
  • Don't wait until you're almost out of cash to find an ATM — convenience stores are everywhere, but it's one less thing to think about if you top up earlier in the day.
  • Keep your card and passport handy separately; some exchange shops and banks ask for ID even when they don't strictly require it.

Cash vs. card vs. ATM vs. WOWPASS

Option Typical cost Works everywhere? Best for
Cash (Myeongdong exchange shop) Best rate of any walk-in option, no extra fee Yes Markets, street food, small local shops
Visa/Mastercard/UnionPay Often 1–3% foreign transaction fee from your home bank Most places, not all Everyday spending in cities and tourist areas
Global ATM withdrawal ~₩3,000–4,000 per withdrawal + your bank's fee Anywhere with a Global ATM Topping up cash quickly, mid-market rate with cards like Wise
WOWPASS No foreign transaction fee, competitive exchange rate Domestic-network terminals + transit Travelers who want one card for both payments and T-money

💬 Still not sure how much cash to bring or which card to use? Tell us your trip length and where you're headed in the comments, and we'll help you plan it out!
meta_description: A first-timer's guide to exchanging cash, using Visa/Mastercard, and withdrawing Korean won from ATMs in South Korea, plus WOWPASS as a card alternative.
